Before you report the bill, Mr. Chairman, may I direct the attention of the committee to something most extraordinary. Very often it is impossible for the comptroller of the treasury to check the revenue from each tax. In connection with some taxes the Department of National Revenue, both excise and customs branches, have difficulty in indicating the amounts derived therefrom. That is very extraordinary. It seems to me there could be a way of informing people about it. Each tax brings in a certain definite amount, and any person asking for the amount derived from a certain tax should be able to get that information. The condition is unbelievable, but I could bring the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue to several returns I got last year in which there were certificates from excise and customs commissioners to the effect that they were unable to state the exact amount of one tax for several years. That is a most interesting situation, because it related to the taxation imposed by that super-genius in financial matters, the ex-Prime Minister. Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 97, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reason for the amendment is set forth in a communication I received some time ago from Mr. Sedgewick, chief commissioner of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission. I think it well to put the communication on record. It is as follows:
Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Canada
Ottawa, May the 6th, 1936. Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, P.C., Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
My Dear Prime Minister:-
I have observed that in your statement to the house of the business to come before it this session you mentioned a possible amendment to the Combines Investigation Act. I have frequently discussed the matter of amendments with Mr. McGregor and there are a number of amendments which, in our opinion, would be advisable but we feel that there is one which is a necessity if any investigations are to be made under the Combines Investigation Act. In my opinion it -would be absolutely unsafe to go on with an investigation-at least an investigation which might be expected to result in a criminal prosecution-without an amendment to section 24 of the act. This section was amended in the dying days of the last session in the Senate and the House of Commons concurred in the amendment, very possibly without having had any real opportunity to consider it. In the result, documents which the investigator, under the Combines Investigation Act, might require to have produced to him in his investigation would be privileged and not admissible against the offender in a subsequent prosecution if section 24 remains in its present position. The section as it stands now is as follows:
"24. No person shall be excused from attending and giving evidence and producing books, papers, or records, in obedience to the order of the commission, on the ground that the oral evidence or documents required of him may tend to criminate him or subject him to any proceeding or penalty, but no such evidence or documents so required shall be used or receivable against such person in any criminal proceedings thereafter instituted against him, other than a prosecution for perjury in giving evidence upon such investigation, inquiry, cause or proceeding. 1923, c. 9. s. 18; R.S., 1927. c. 26, s. 24; 1935, c. 54, s. 17."
If your memory wdll carry you back to the Combines Investigation Act when it was introduced in 1923, you will perhaps recall that the corresponding section as the act was drafted was in substantially the form of section 24 as it now exists but as the bill was going through the house you had the section amended to strike out the words "or documents," as it appears now in line six of section 24, and inserted the word "oral" before "evidence," which latter word is now the first word in the sixth line.
I am quite satisfied in my own mind that the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission -of which I am Chief Commissioner-would not risk having an investigator require the production of any documents until this act is amended.
I hope it may not be considered presumption on my part to say the amendment suggested is indispensable to a proper administration of the Combines Investigation Act.
Yours faithfully,
George H. Sedgewick,
Chief Commissioner.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND ASSISTANCE ACT, 1936, TO ASSIST PROVINCES IN RESPECT OF RELIEF EXPENDITURES

speechtext:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:	.
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend section four of The Unemployment Belief and Assistance Act, 1936, being chapter fifteen of the statutes of 1936, to empower the governor in council to grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance or guarantee to an amount not exceeding the amount payable by the province for its share of the cost of unemployment relief and undertakings during February and March, 1936, and under any agreement between the dominion and the province entered into under the authority of the said act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND ASSISTANCE ACT, 1936, TO ASSIST PROVINCES IN RESPECT OF RELIEF EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when bill No. 19, the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act, 1936, was drafted, it was proposed to obtain from parliament authority

for the governor in council to grant, where necessary, financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance or guarantee, of a total amount not in excess of the total amount payable by the dominion to such province under any agreement entered into under the authority of the act. The assistance was thought at that time to be sufficient to meet the relief requirements of the various provinces, and consequently section 4 of the act was so worded.
However, in the case of one or two of the western provinces no arrangement had been made at the expiry date of the Relief Act, 1935, for financing their relief requirements for February and March and applications to the dominion for assistance for those months were received too late to be dealt with under that authority. I may say that the requests were in connection with loans that were naturally subsequent to expenditures for relief and, therefore, the applications for loans for those particular months arrived at a date following the expiry of the Relief Act, 1935 In addition, representations have been made that the provincial share of relief outlays in some cases exceeded the total amount payable by the dominion under agreements entered into under the authority of the act. For these reasons it is considered necessary to establish a new criterion, as it were, for loans to be made to the provinces for relief purposes. Under the bill which will be founded upon this resolution there will be an amendment of section 4 only of the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act, 1936. As proposed in this resolution, the dominion will be empowered to grant financial assistance where necessary to any province of its share of expenditures for relief and relief undertakings during February and March 19(36, and under any agreement which may be entered into under the authority of the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act, 1936.

The comparison which
the hon. gentleman has instituted between disarmament and this particular matter has of course some striking features. Is the federal treasury to be disarmed for the purpose of

Unemployment-Relief Expenditures
enabling raids upon it to be carried out successfully? I judged from what the hon. gentleman said on a previous occasion that it was to safeguard the federal treasury against the attacks that might be made against it that he had provided it with such heavy armament that there was no doubt the defence would be complete. I judge from what he says now, having regard to the analogy he has sought to make, that he has concluded that his armament is entirely too heavy and that he must dispense with some of his heavier artillery and some of his guns with a view to facilitating the approach of the enemy. That is the only conclusion one can draw from the observations he has made. The blank cheque does not cease to be a blank cheque because there is an ultimate restriction placed upon it. When the hon. gentleman said that my own close knowledge of the situation was sufficient to induce me to believe that the matter was a difficult one to deal with, I can only say that is quite true. But I hardly expected to have the recognition of it come from the source from which it does; that was wholly unexpected. It is an occasion for gratification to think that it took an amendment to a bill passed this session to enable the hon. gentleman to make the discovery, and I trust that as he proceeds in the administration of the department he will have some sympathy with those who were charged with responsibility on a previous occasion; and more numerous will be the instances in which he will realize that the policies which were followed by them were policies to which he himself has given and is giving adherence. The limitation placed upon armament is of course, shall I say, somewhat elastic because it leaves the expenditure with the province. Surely it would be possible to arrive at an amount not exceeding so much money in view of the known experience of, say, the four years during which one had fairly complete knowledge of what was being done by the various provinces. Would it not be possible to have such a sum, not exceeding so many millions of dollars? Would that not have been a quantitative restriction upon the amount, which would have been perhaps very valuable armament for the federal treasury as against the attacks to which the hon. gentleman has referred? And possibly the amount named would have to be such as to make it undoubted that it would meet the requirements of the situation. It will be remembered that during one of the years we did place first of all a quantitative restriction and that latterly, owing to the attitude taken by the then opposition, there was a limitation placed upon the amount that might be used for relief by the dominion.

There is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. When the federal government grants relief to provinces there ought to be some greater check on the action of the provinces, some assurance that the people who are in need will receive an adequate scale of relief. The provinces seem to leave the matter to the municipalities; in some municipalities at least the scales of relief are very low, and sometimes certain classes are discriminated against. I had a case the other day

if my memory serves me correctly it was from a town in western Ontario-in which relief was refused to one or two young people in the home because the mother was in receipt of old age pension. The old age pension originally of course was a matter of dominion legislation. I think it comes under the administration of the Minister of Finance as far as this government is concerned. I know the detailed administration is by the provinces. Certainly when we passed that legislation some years ago the idea was that the old people would be entitled to the benefit of that pension for themselves. In this case a poor old woman's pension was diminished on account of her having to keep one of her sons who otherwise would have gone on relief. I think in such cases the dominion government ought to insist that the purpose of the old age pension legislation be carried out, and that the giving of relief be on a scale adequate to the maintenance of something like a decent standard of living. I know there are difficulties, but some of us get a great many complaints of this kind, and I think the dominion government should insist on adequate standards and a better system of relief than prevails in some municipalities.

Earlier in the session I introduced a bill to postpone the annual revision of the closed lists. The house agreed to that bill, but it was also agreed that if the special committee dealing with the elections and franchise acts was not in a position to report and recommend the adoption of a general act at the present session, we would make provision either to revise or to prepare lists for by-elections. speechtext: With the consent of the committee, the hon. member may proceed.

I shall not delay consideration of the measure. Section 3 refers to the supplying of copies of lists of electors and the supplying of election material, all of which is dependent upon the provision appearing at the bottom of page 2 of the bill. Paragraph (D) (4) is as follows:
(4) If the polling division is urban, the returning officer shall prepare from the geographical list of electors a separate list for each polling station established therein. The list shall be divided numerically according to the consecutive number given to each voter on the printed list of electors so that approximately an equal number of electors will be allotted to each polling station necessarily established in such polling division.
By looking at the opposite page hon. members will see that for the geographical list there is substituted another list prepared alphabetically. I wish to oppose any substitution for the geographical list. I cannot deal with the conditions obtaining in any other city; my intimate knowledge is confined to conditions in one electoral district of one city, but I do say that the geographical list as prepared and used at the polls in each polling division has to a very large extent prevented frauds. Further it has prevented impersonation. I have no hesitation in saying that in times past in the city of Montreal impersonation has been carried to an extent not known in any other city in Canada. Although I do not speak from personal knowledge, I know that following one election in which I took part an examination of the returns disclosed, to the satisfaction of competent men reviewing the situation, that at least a thousand impersonations had been carried out in the electoral district of St. Lawrence-St. George. That is a condition of affairs against which every possible protective provision should be enacted.
The adoption of the geographical list enables an inspection of the list to determine who are registered for each particular building or apartment house. For instance, in one of my elections, before the geographical list was adopted, an unfortunate circumstance arose in connection with an eminent clergyman, one of the most respected of the Catholic clergy of Montreal. He had provided for a hostel for young men from outside the city attending universities in Montreal. It was an enterprise which was most advantageous for parents in the country who are sending 12739-233 J
their sons either to Catholic or to Protestant schools, because in law and in scientific departments many Catholic students attended McGill university as well as the university of Montreal. When the names are on the list and classified according to letter, without considerable research it is difficult to ascertain what names appear for a particular address. In one of my elections through careful investigation we sifted out the facts and found that for this residence for students attending the universities fifty-six names had been added to the list, and they were names of persons who had not been known as residents in that place. When names are registered geographically such frauds are easily perceived, and the proper oath may be administered to the applicants for voting as they appear.
I should dislike very much to see the geographical list abandoned, either at the polls or in the preparation of the lists. Enumerators proceeding along the street can easily prepare their returns in geographical sequence, because they enter one house after the other, and turn in the names in that order. If the change at the bottom of page 2 and the top of page 3 of the bill means that the geographic list is to be abandoned or limited in any way, I am very much opposed to it.

The objection to the act of 1934, if it had remained as it stood, was that we were afraid a general revision would be very costly and would achieve little purpose because the electors would not avail themselves of the opportunity of revision if no special election were in view in their particular constituency. At the same time the committee did not recommend local revision where a by-election is to take place. It has recommended the preparation of mew lists, and in making such recommendation the committee has had in view the saving of time. That is why in certain clauses of the bill changes have been made, to save time and facilitate matters.
I might also point out that the committee has recommended a couple of changes in Bill No. 78, which we are now considering. One restores in rural polling divisions the right of an elector whose name does not appear on the list to present himself at the poll and take oath and vote. That right did exist under former electoral acts. The other change does away with the absentee vote.
As to the particular section to which my hon. friend referred, again I wish to say that the idea that seems to have actuated the committee was to facilitate the preparation of special lists for by-elections. I have notes here on that particular section which indicate that in this case the change has been made for the convenience of election officials, and it will be noted that it will apply only to cases in which there are two or more polling stations in the same polling division. That is to say, if in a certain polling division the number of electors is too large to have it kept single, and it is necessary to divide it in two, then it is provided by this amendment that a list may be prepared in a numerical way, doing away with the more complicated system of having both numerical and geographical lists. I do not think there can be much objection to that. It will apply only in exceptional cases where subdivisions must be established by the electoral officer in one polling division, but it does not do away, if I understand the amendment correctly, with the former method of preparing lists in polling divisions at large.

Let me say to my hon.
friend that I can deal from personal knowledge only with St. Lawrence-St. George. In that district nearly every polling division has to be divided into subdivisions for the purpose of polling, but that does not necessitate any doing away with the preparation of the lists according to streets and numbers. The procedure which is followed under the existing law is that the lists are prepared street by 
street, with each number in sequence. What is the number that may be permitted for the poll? Is it three hundred?
I think it is three hundred.

If it runs over three hundred, all that the official has to do is to post up a notice and say that the names on the list from such and such down to such and such, perhaps half way down the list, will vote in polling booth No. 1; and the others will vote in polling booth No. 2, and almost invariably polling booths No. 1 and No. 2 are in the same building, on either side of the hall of entry. But if you do away with the preparation of the lists of names according to the geographical sequence, you facilitate fraud in the constituencies of which I know, to an extent that has not prevailed in recent elections. It is monstrous that impersonation should be possible under any election act to the extent to which it has prevailed in some of the constituencies of which I know. It is not for me to go into local affairs, but the preparation of the geographical list prevented in the constituency of which I know the recurrence of frauds perpetrated under the local list-

Does this amendment
take that away?
I do not know.

I might draw the hon.
member's attention to the provision in the amendment to the Franchise Act, Bill No. 81. We still make up the geographical list in the same way as the list was prepared under the original bill.

But what do you do with
it?

it is sent to the
returning officer. I will read the section:

Such list shall be prepared in all urban polling divisions in geographical order, that is, by streets, roads and avenues, as in Form No. 7. from Bill No. 78, the one we are considering. That geographical list is not the list used at the polling.

Section 3 (D) provides:
If the polling division is urban, the returning officer shall prepare from the geographical list of electors a separate list for each polling station established therein.
He has to take that from the geographical list.

He has not to prepare a
separate list. There is no reason in the world why he should do it. The geographical list is there; it is printed, and all he has to do is as he has done in the preceding elections, say that those on the list, from such a number down to such a number in a certain polling division will go into No. 1 booth to vote.

Does this section
change that? It is not the intention to change it.

In other words, the list which you prepare from the enumerators is a geographical list, and that is the list for the elections at the present time. Here you say that although you have gone to the expense of preparing a geographical list for the purpose of voting in any polling station, which has to be subdivided into two or three polling booths, a new list shall be prepared. Instead of saving money, it seems to me that new expenditures will have to be made and that the new list will have to be renumbered. The result is that it will be almost impossible for the officials at the polling booth to keep a careful count of those who are entitled to vote and their places of residence, as registered. We are not eliminating any expenditure. At the bottom of page 2 you provide for striking out subsections 4 and 6 of section 33 of the present act, and for making substitutions therefor. I suggest that there is no need to strike out those subsections when you have the other section in the Franchise Act providing for a geographical list. If it is thought that that should be amended, let us amend it. I do not know whether the chairman of this committee represents a rural or an urban riding.

I can quite realize that the bon. member would not appreciate the difficulties with which we are confronted in urban districts.
Some members of the committee represented urban ridings.
Did they come from Montreal?

In view of the conditions which prevailed in the city of Montreal I cannot understand why any urban representative should ask for a change. I do not think any representative from the city of Montreal can stand in his place and say, so far as the preparation of the lists and the administration of the electoral acts were concerned during the last general elections, they were not administered with a propriety and exactitude and fairness unprecedented in the recent electoral history of that city. Why break down these barriers to fraud and misrepresentation?

If I thought that that section would have the effect that my hon. friend thinks it will have, I would not endorse it. I hope the committee understands my position. This bill was not prepared by myself or by the officials of my department; it has been recommended unanimously by a committee of the house consisting of both urban and rural members from all parties. I must say that I fail to see in this section the danger pointed out by my hon. friend. We are discussing this bill in somewhat piecemeal fashion, but let me point out that the lists will be prepared-
Geographically.

In geographical order. Where the lists are prepared and at the last moment, perhaps a few days before nomination, the returning officer finds that in a certain polling division he has more than the required number of electors, he is allowed by this section to prepare a numerical list for that subdivision or polling station. My hon. friend says that in his constituency that procedure would be pretty general, but I believe in most of our city ridings this would not happen more than about once in forty or fifty polling divisions.
I do not agree with that.

Section 3 provides for the preparation of special lists for a by-election. The committee has recommended that a polling division shall be the polling division adopted on the occasion of the dominion general elections held on October 14, 1935. A writ is issued and lists are prepared according to the polling divisions which obtained at the last general election. The enumerators do their work and lists are prepared a few days before nomination day. The returning officers have to subdivide a certain number of polling stations. I disagree with the hon. mem-
Elections Act

ber for St. Lawrence-St. George as to the number of stations in connection with which this would be necessary. From my experience I believe this will happen in only a few oases. In order to save time the returning officer can prepare numerical lists for voting. I cannot see any danger in procedure such as that, because it will be only exceptional. I believe that the committee in submitting this bill and the one that follows had in mind the fact that it might be preferable to make this experiment in a by-election to incorporating the changes in the general act when it is revised. This is not my proposal; it is a proposal unanimously recommended by a committee composed of members from all sides of the house.
Like my colleague, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), I had some doubt about this, but I think if one reads it carefully he will see that the geographical list obtains.
Quite so, in the first preparation.

First of all we have provided that the same polling divisions shall obtain in a bynelection as obtained in the last general election. That is number one; that is settled. Second, the Franchise Act provides for the preparation of lists, and it follows the same provision with respect to geographical locations as were followed in 1935. I thought there was some doubt about that, but it is clear beyond peradventure. We come now to the next point about which we had some doubt. The returning officer, whose duty is defined by the statute, receives the list. Some confusion arose, at least in my mind, as between a polling station and a polling division. The polling division has not been changed from what it was in 1935, but the polling station may be. It states on page 3 of the bill:
_ The list shall be divided numerically according to the consecutive number given to each voter on the printed list of electors so that approximately an equal number of electors will be allotted to each polling station necessarily established in such polling division.
That is, there may be 300 in a division and the effort of the returning officer may be to divide that into two stations of 150 each, or into three stations of 100 each. On the opposite page appear the details as to how the list is made up by the franchise officer. The geographical conditions of the Franchise Act are continued and have not been changed.
I think that is fairly clear. At first I had some doubt about it, but I think it is clear.
fMr. Riafret.]

May I give an explanation of this section? I had some part in drafting it and to me it is clear. It is the same procedure that was followed in the last general election. The lists are prepared, and where there are more than 300 names at any poll the returning officer divides it in two. In my own riding, if I remember rightly, there were 131 polls, but on election day the returning officer, finding over 60 of these polls with more than 300 names, divided each of these in two- On page 28 of the franchise bill we find a sample page of a voters' list. In many of the polling subdivisions in my riding there were over 400 names and the lists were divided as on page 28. If we take that as an example, that page has only 50 names. If the allotment per poll were 50 instead of 300, and if the returning officer followed the procedure of the last election, dividing the poll in two, each poll would have 25.

I can clear that up in a moment. This is only a sample, and it is not intended to apply to 50 names. Fifty have been given merely as an illustration, but the list would contain many more names than that.

The list may have anywhere from 300 to 500 names. It is provided that if the polling substation is urban the returning officer shall follow the geographical list. There is no intention of changing from the present geographical method; that remains in the act. He has to prepare a separate list for each polling subdivision and these shall be divided numerically. That is the way it was done the last time; I do not see any change.

I appreciate the fact
that to have the general aspect of both pieces of legislation it might have been advisable to do what we have been doing so far. But we are not only going from one section to another but from one bill to the other. Perhaps now that we have discussed the general principle the chairman will call the sections one by one. This discussion has taken place on section 1, the short title, which I suppose carries.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Amendments to apply in the case of by-elections.

Section 2 provides that all amendments in this bill, the provisions of the general act, "are not amended, repealed

Elections Act
or otherwise affected by the provisions of this act except in so far as the holding of byelections is concerned."

Section agreed to.
On section 3-By-elections.

This section provides that the polling divisions shall be those established for the last general election. Paragraph (B) permits the transfer of lists and copies of lists from the franchise officer to the returning officer without the necessity of sending them to the central office in Ottawa. That is to save time in remote parts of the country. Paragraph (C) proposes some minor changes in order to make the general act apply to by-elections. Paragraph (D)(4) is the one we have been discussing, and I understand it has been agreed to. Paragraph (E) does away with the disposition which was necessary in the general act and which should not apply in by-elections, the provision whereby, when an elector moved from one constituency to another, if he were not qualified to vote in the new one he would retain his right to vote in the constituency he had just left. In by-elections, the committee has suggested, no one should be qualified to be on the list unless he has resided three months in the polling division where the by-election is held. Paragraph (F) reestablishes the principle whereby in rural constituencies an elector who is not on the list may come to the poll and be vouched for, a note being made that he is entitled to vote. Paragraph (G) strikes out all the sections with respect to the absentee vote. The committee did not regard it as having been a great success, but no matter what opinion one may have on that point I think we can all agree that there should not be absentee votes in a by-election. Paragraph (H) modifies four different forms so as to make them applicable to the purposes of this bill.

I do not think that the
explanations given by the minister are altogether satisfactory. What I am insisting on is that the list of voters for each polling station, which is used by the officials at that polling station, shall be a geographical list. In the elections which were held in some of the cities at the last general election I should think that at least sixty out of ninety polling divisions were found to include a larger number than three hundred, which I believe is the limit, and therefore a division was necessary. No separate list was prepared in a different numerical order, but the deputy returning officer took the
printed list and counted down to half of that list and then gave the first half to a polling station which he called polling booth "A" and the other half to another polling station which he called polling booth "B," which were both usually in the same building. But the geographical sequence of the names was continued for each list so dealt with and no separate printing nor separate typewriting for the urban district was necessary at any time. Paragraph (D) on page 2 reads:
If the polling division is urban, the returning officer shall prepare from the geographical list of electors a separate list for each polling station established therein.
What I wish to make clear is that such list Shall be prepared geographically and divided numerically according to the consecutive numbers given to each voter on the printed geographical list. From the time the first list is made up in geographical order to the time of polling, the list prepared for the officer in each polling booth should be geographical. Otherwise it is impossible to protect the polls. If my hon. friend is prepared to admit that this list shall be prepared geographically and then divided numerically according to the consecutive numbers in that printed list, I am content.

Perhaps I might explain. At page 36 of the Franchise Act the geographical list is dealt with, and every voter gets a number on that list. The voters are numbered consecutively. When it comes to dividing that list as between polling stations the returning officer simply takes the first half of the list, we shall say-
That is what he should do.
That is exactly what is intended by this section.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me, we took particular pains in the sections which are being repealed to show that this subdivision must be made in such a way that when divided the lists would be geographical. Now you have struck that out. If you will make it clear that this list so divided shall be a geographical list and divided numerically according to the printed geographical list, I am content, but to leave it in doubt-
I do not think there is any doubt.

Perhaps my hon. friend will agree to this proposal: This bill applies only to by-elections, and for all we know there might not be one by-election in an urban centre during the year. The committee
Elections Act

was unanimous in recommending these amendments, and I may say that the chief electoral officer informed me that this would mean a considerable saving of time, as well as being a much simpler way of dealing with the matter. There might be very few polling stations, perhaps none, where this would apply during the coming year. My hon. friend has registered his protest. It is possible that the committee may have overlooked his point, but I believe the committee went into these questions pretty carefully, and these amendments were recommended unanimously. My hon. friend differs in opinion with the committee. Why not try this out? As I say, it will apply only in exceptional cases; it is intended to save time, and it has been recommended not by one party but by representatives of all parties. I should be averse to making any alterations of such a kind in a bill which has been unanimously recommended by representatives of all sides of the house. Of course my hon. friend has a perfect right and is quite in order to discuss every section of the bill, but apparently his views on this point, though strong, are to some extent personal. He has registered his protest and made his remarks, and now perhaps the committee will agree to pass the bill as it has been recommended. If we find that there is actually any point to my hon. friend's remarks, when the committee deals with the general act next year they may pay heed to the representations which have been made this afternoon.

If the statement made by
the hon. member for Swift Current, who was chairman of that committee, is correct, then my suggestion simply makes very clear the purpose and intent of the committee which prepared this amendment. There is no doubt about that. I am not urging any change in the intent and purpose of this amendment as stated by the chairman of the committee, and therefore I do not feel that in pressing for a clarification of these two lines I am attempting to disparage the deliberate judgment of the committee. I have no such intention. The hon. gentleman says that he proposes to save some expense by not carrying out my suggestion. There is no possibility of saving expense-

I said that time would
be saved.

The hon. gentleman says that this is a personal matter with me. I am simply giving my experience. It is not personal. If it is made clear that this list for each polling booth is to be a geographical list, numbered consecutively according to the geographical list first prepared, I shall accept it, but I think I might fairly ask to have this line amended in order to make that perfectly clear.

Before we let it stand may I say that the period of three months is too long. First, we have three months before the issue of the writ, and a time after that which is very often as long as sixty days, making five months. In a place where there is a large floating population'-and I have in mind the logging camps in my constituency-an unfair situation is created. It means that large numbers will be disfranchised. Prior to the act passed in 1935, a period of sixty days before the date of election was provided. That was considered a reasonable and fair

I believe the committee considered that it should not depart too much from the act of 1934, in which the period of three months is indicated. Of course at the time of a general election, if an elector cannot qualify in one constituency he does in another. In this instance the special provision is that unless he has resided at a certain place three months before the issuing of the writ in the constituency where the by-election is held, he is not qualified to vote. I think there is some wisdom in not drifting too far from the general act, except as to adapting it to by-elections. Evidently that is the reason the three months' qualification has been retained. Under the Dominion

I believe that is a wise provision, in any case. I found in the revision in the St. Lawrence-St. George constituency enumerators attested that within one moving period there were 5,300 changes, and of that

The house resumed from Thursday June 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 53, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934- Mr. Howe-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.

I think the minister
appreciates the fact that this creates a difficult situation. This bill confers upon him the powers which I mentioned yesterday and, taken in conjunction with the other provisions of the act, places him in the invidious position of having to decide for or against the applications which he will receive for the declaration of certain areas as sheltered waters. Not that that in itself is so very important, but it lays the foundation for the application for temporary certificates for navigation. It is not the thing itself; it is what the thing lays the foundation for. Another section provides for an extension for five years of the time mentioned in the act for the qualifying for a certificate. Then there is a provision providing for temporary certificates to be based upon the right to navigate in sheltered waters, which waters are declared to be sheltered by reason of the action taken by the minister. The minister has said that certain action is taken in other places with respect to that and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said that it applies only to ships of small tonnage. The new bill refers to ships of tonnage larger than five tons; in fact temporary certificates may be issued in connection with ships as large as twenty tons. What has been said with respect to small vessels under the control of those who have local knowledge, of course is true. However, sometimes that knowledge is not unlike that of the man who undertook to take a large ship up a narrow river. The master of the ship said to the pilot, "You have a very intimate knowledge of this river?" The pilot said, "Yes, I know all the sand-bars in it; this is one now." Just then the ship struck a sand-bar. This lays the foundation for great abuse, and it is my duty to point it out. I know the minister, in view of what he said yesterday, will not care to adopt the only remedy.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Marine):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I quite appreciate that the Minister of Marine is being given very great power, but I really see no alternative. In fact, I think very few people understand the power that the Minister of Marine has in this case. For instance, all the inspectors in Canada can declare a ship to be unseaworthy,
Canada Shipping Act

and the minister can declare it to be seaworthy. The minister has the power of licensing everyone that has to do with the sea.
And suspending.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: And suspending. As I see it, this matter of minor waters must be regularized. For the last twenty-seven years we have been administering a great number of harbours on the east and west coasts as minor waters without a vestige of authority for so doing. For instance, on the British Columbia coast we have Burrard inlet, east of the First Narrows, and the northeast arm of Quatsino sound inside Limestone island, and the eastern channel, Barclay sound. On the Atlantic coast there are some twenty harbours and waters of various kinds which have been administered as minor waters, although by every law in the statute books they are major waters and can be navigated only by mariners having deep sea certificates. In both England and the United States this same authority is vested in one man, and if my right hon. friend could suggest a better way for Canada we should be glad to consider it. Through a curious anomaly the lighthouse board, a board of departmental officials, have authority under the law to declare certain coastal waters minor waters for the purpose of administering the life saving act. But there is no authority whatever for declaring coastal waters minor waters for the main purpose of the Canada Shipping Act. The only purpose of this clause is to correct an anomaly in the act, and I think we are doing this in the only practical way.

The minister and the
committee are losing sight of the real reason why very great care should be taken in a measure of this kind, namely, the safety of passengers carried on ships. Apart from that, the matter is a comparatively insignificant one. I do not know whether I can make myself clear, because there are many technicalities involved which I am not qualified to discuss. But the point I wish to make is that for the purpose of meeting the convenience of the owner of a small boat operating in an enclosed water, certainly, in my opinion at any rate, we ought not to give this sweeping power to the minister to declare an area a sheltered water. I say that for this reason. The only criticism which the owner of a small boat has is that if he wants to carry passengers he must have a certified officer if his boat weighs more than five tons. If it weighs 4-99 tons he may carry thirty or forty passengers. Both these conditions are wrong. It does not make it any safer for passengers, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) pointed out, if the boat is 4-99 tons than if

it is five tons. As the hon. gentleman suggested, the owner might remove some of the upper structure so as to bring the boat within the required measurement. In my opinion the measurement of the boat should not be the basis upon which the owner should be allowed to carry passengers. That is the first point I make, and t.he second point is that we certainly should not make it possible for an individual to carry passengers on a boat, which at present he cannot do, simply by declaring that he is operating in minor waters. I shall use the very citation which the minister gave last night and to which he has referred to-day, namely, Burrard inlet. Burrard inlet, stretching from the First Narrows some twenty-five miles into the north arm and into the head of the inlet, is one of the most important seaways in this country. I do not believe there is a port in Canada, not even Montreal, through which a larger number of deep sea vessels pass during the year. For seven months of the year there may be more vessels in some of the other ports, but I mean throughout the year. These deep sea vessels go through the narrows, operating in the first two or three miles of the harbour, now described as minor waters. Deep sea vessels, and particularly coastal vessels that operate like passenger trains on fixed schedules, come in by the dozen every day and operate in that harbour very often in a fog, when the only direction for vessels is the signal given by blowing the whistle. Yet we are allowing persons who have no master's certificate, no deep sea experience, very little knowledge of deep sea signalling or navigation, to carry passengers, provided their boats are under five tons. Under this proposal, because this area is declared to comprise minor waters, the owner of a boat under five tons may be allowed to carry passengers, though the area is highly dangerous.
With a certificate.

Not necessarily, if the area is declared, as this amendment makes it, a minor water. If it is a minor water he may carry passengers. What I am driving at is this: Above everything else we ought to safeguard the lives of people, and if a man has a boat and wishes to carry passengers he ought at least to undertake the responsibility of having a certified officer on board. The owner of a small boat may know the waters well; he operates here and there along the coast; and on a holiday he wishes to carry a few passengers and cannot do so. The argument may be that he knows more about handling that little boat than anybody else. Usually that class of boat is used for roustabout purposes at logging camps or round a cannery or

Canada Shipping Act
some small settlement in an inlet, and for such purposes, carrying a little freight, it is perfectly satisfactory. But the moment the owner wants to carry passengers even, as suggested by my hon. friend from Comox-Al-bemi, across the inlet, I do not care under what conditions, we cannot be too careful in seeing to it that such a person is licensed only under such terms as shall ensure the maximum of safety and efficiency. That is the reason I question this method.
The hon. gentleman overlooks section 122 of the shipping act.

I suggest to the minister, therefore, that whether or not he drops the words with regard to sheltered waters to be specified by him-and I think they should be dropped-we should specify more clearly the conditions under which any ship may carry passengers, whether it be a vessel of fifteen tons or over, or five tons or under. There have been tragic accidents in years gone by, partly through inexperience. While it is all very well to say that there are many men who have masters' certificates, though they have not been at sea, although that sounds well, there are those who may operate their vessels recklessly, and I submit that recklessness should not be allowed in the carrying of passengers, no matter whether the waters are declared minor or otherwise.

At six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was practically through what I had to say. I should like to remind the minister, however, of the point I was making, namely that taking power to declare certain waters on the coasts of Canada as minor waters, such power being vested in the minister, was not the proper basis upon which the whole problem should be considered. I had pointed out that in my opinion the attention of the committee and of the minister and his officials should be focussed upon the fact that the carriage of passengers is really the crucial point. I am aware that under section 122 of the main act provision is made for temporary certificates to be issued to individuals in charge of vessels not over twenty tons and not carrying more than twelve passengers. But in my opinion that does not meet the ease. An excellent suggestion has been made by the Canadian Merchant Service Guild in Vancouver. They say that these small boats could be classed as ferries, and that one of the qualifications for a certificate for a man operating a ferry under fifteen tons should be that the applicant has had at least twelve months' service on a coasting or ocean-going vessel under a certificated master, so assuring that he has had some experience and training. Now, that is a limited request. A man who operates a small ferry in minor waters, which minor waters, to take Burrard inlet as an illustration, may be daily traversed by dozens of coastwise and deep sea ships, in fog or stormy conditions or where tidal currents prevail-a man operating a ferry under such conditions should at least have a working acquaintance with coastwise or deep sea practice.
That approach to the question is, to my mind, the correct one. I would plead with the minister earnestly not to take it amiss that we suggest that this is perhaps the wrong way of dealing with these minor waters. It is no reflection upon him to say so. As he said himself this afternoon, ministers are sometimes clothed with extraordinary authority, but it is generally understood that they exercise only that authority on competent advice. He very properly says-and I appreci-
Canada Shipping Act

ate it-that he has no idea of using that power in any reckless way. No one suggests that at all. But in my opinion it will not meet the situation which is in the mind of those who are urging this amendment. So I conclude with just these observations: first, it is unwise to leave the naming of minor waters wide open in that way. I think there should be greater restrictions in that respect. If possible it should be a statutory matter. The other point, which to my mind is much more important, is that in regard to the complaints or requests of those who operate casually what we may call small boats in what they allege to be minor waters, their case should be considered only or chiefly in the light of the safety of passengers. I appreciated the words of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) the other evening and I am quite well acquainted with the circumstances which I think he had in mind, in the remoter sections of the Pacific coast, with its innumerable inlets. Men who unquestionably are well skilled in handling boats may occasionally get an opportunity to carry pasengers. While I have a great deal of sympathy with the suggestion that men of that type should be assisted in every way, nevertheless I lay this down as extremely important, that the question of safety must be kept in mind. I can easily understand how a man who might operate one of these small boats in freighting, roustabout work, in the language of the trade, might be quite efficient in that, and he takes his own chances, but it is a different matter when a man' of that type is entrusted with the lives of ten or twenty or thirty passengers. I find myself very strongly of the opinion that the suggestion of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild should be given very careful consideration.
My hon. friend spoke of his experience with the Indians in canoes. It is, I think, forty years ago that I was largely responsible for navigating a small vessel for four or five hundred miles up the coast. We got along very well; there were four or five of us on board; we went hither and thither without charts or much equipment of that kind, but no one could argue that the fact that a person acquires in that way a knowledge of the coast and of the general handling of a boat, qualifies him to have the responsibility of carrying passengers in such a boat. It is from that angle that I have presented these arguments, and request the minister to give consideration to the suggestions of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild as well as my own.

My chief interest is in the ferries operating from Vancouver to North Vancouver, and through the First Narrows to West Vancouver. The minister must appreciate that the navigation of those waters is extremely dangerous, particularly in foggy weather. Has the minister considered whether or not it might be preferable to use the expression "smooth waters" instead of "sheltered waters." After all, this question is of vital importance to us on the Pacific coast, because most of the mainland coast might be considered as Sheltered by Vancouver island or the Queen Charlotte islands. Then, we have very large inlets, which are really great arms of the sea. I think the expression "sheltered waters" is too wide. "Smooth waters" would be much better. I suggest that this provision is particularly important as it applies to the waters around the city of Vancouver, because there are many thousands of people travelling on those waters. The situation is quite different from that in Comox-Alberni where people will know those operators who understand boats and those who do not. On the other hand many people will be carried as passengers on the ferries operating around Vancouver, believing that they are protected by government regulations and are being transported by duly qualified men. I would suggest using the expression "smooth waters" instead of "sheltered waters," and considering the possibility of deleting the word "inlets." It is a really serious question on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It makes no difference what we call them. We declare what they are by law. In England it is the practice to call them smooth waters, while in Canada and in the United States it is customary to call them minor waters. speechtext: No, not at all.

Mr. Chairman, I have in mind a matter which should be considered in connection with this bill. To a great extent the Canada Shipping Act has been copied from the British Shipping Act, but there is a great difference between Canadian shipping and British shipping. The British Isles are in the middle of the Atlantic ocean-
When were they moved?

They are not in the
middle, but they are in the Atlantic ocean.

In Canada we have an entirely different situation, because we have inland navigation. For these reasons amendments concerning minor waters are of great importance. A certificate is required from captains, and in the issuance of such certificates the experience of the captain in matters of navigation should be the chief concern. When it is proved satisfactorily that a man has been in charge of a boat in such minor waters of Canada for several years, and he has shown his competence as a captain, I do not see why his certificate should be refused on technical grounds.
There is another point to consider, something which in my mind is just as important as the competence of the captain in charge of the ship. My point is that in inland waters where navigation takes place there should be lights on all wharves. May I bring anew to the attention of the minister the following facts: One of those minor waters of Canada is lake Temiscouata, a body of water twenty-seven miles long and a mile and a quarter wide. On the lake there are five wharves, and back of it, in the back country there are many settlements. To reach those settlements one must cross the lake, first from Cabano to Squatteck, and, second, from Notre Dame du Lac to St. Juste du Lac. In connection with the latter point there are two wharves, one being at St. Juste du Lac and the other at Route Centrale. Navigation is more difficult because there are no lights on those wharves. So much money is expended by the government that I suggest lights should be put on those wharves to facilitate navigation at night. I see the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) in his seat. He is familiar with the geography of that part of the country, and I say to him that if the government is ready to spend a lot of money for delivering mail in the winter time to people who live far away, I do not see why there should not be better facilities for those people who have to cross the lake. As I said previously, there are two ferry services, one between Cabano and Squatteck for the settlement of Squatteck and for people in other settlements east of Squatteck in both Temiscouata and Rimouski constituencies. The nearest doctors are at Cabano, Notre Dame du Lac and St. Louis, west and north of lake Temiscouata. They have to cross the lake to reach those people, and at the present time there are no lights on any of those wharves. When I asked the minister to see to it that lights should be put there, his answer was that nobody would have accepted the position of wharfinger last year. There is a very good reason for that, and it is because all the traffic there is done by the
[Mr. Pouliot.l
settlers, who carry away all their products at once and leave nothing on the wharf. They cannot pay any wharfage charges at all, and no remuneration can be expected from that wharf because the storage amounts to nothing. May I ask the minister if he will kindly see to it that lights are put on those wharves at the expense of the Department of Marine in order to facilitate navigation in minor waters like lake Temiscouata?
May I -also say to the minister that the same thing can be said of the channel between Notre Dame de 1'Isle Verte and the mainland. more time of the committee, but I wish to impress upon the minister that this is a matter of vital importance to many people along the north shore of Burrard inlet, and we feel that so-me greater measure of protection should be given to the travelling public no matter what the size of the vessel may be.
We are particularly vitally concerned as to how these waters may be classified. The minister was good enough to give me some information, but I am still not clear about the matter. He states that these waters must be actually sheltered. That term may be applicable to the waters further north, but not to Burrard inlet, and particularly the waters adjacent to the First Narrows, where there are the dangers of heavy seas, congested sea-going traffic, and fog- The minister also states that it could reasonably be said that Vancouver harbour east of Prospect point-

speechtext:
Will my hon. friend permit
me to interrupt? I had forgotten where Point Atkinson was. Only that part of Burrard inlet east of the First Narrows, is considered sheltered waters, so my hon. friend may disregard the part outside the First Narrows.

Reference has been made
to the Canadian Merchant Service Guild. I know the members of this guild. It is comprised largely of the deck officers of coastal vessels and ferries plying in and out of the harbour of Vancouver, the very men who are most familiar with the hazards of

Caiuida Shipping Act
navigation in that area and who have to take the risk of meeting other craft in charge of inexperienced masters. I think the evidence submitted by this guild should not be disregarded, however expert a knowledge the technical officers of the department may possess. The guild say in their statement to the minister:
We desire to bring to your attention that under the provisions of such an act all the coast of British Columbia, with the exception of a few comparatively short reaches, could be classed as minor waters, which would leave the way open to abuses which could be far-reaching and very dangerous to the sea-borne travelling public; in fact it could be construed in such a manner that the whole effect of the Shipping Act relating to the qualifications and experience necessary to operate coasting vessels would be nullified.
Undoubtedly the act would be administered while the present local officials and administration are in office more in accordance with the intent than the letter of the act, but we think that now is the time to protect and safeguard the future and if possible avoid an undesirable precedent.
You can readily see that, under the provisions of the proposed amendment, Bill 53, the inlets which might, or might not, be classed as minor waters would depend on the opinion of the minister in office, and as it is not likely that successive ministers would always hold the same opinion in this regard, certain inlets might be classed for a period as "minor" and again as "coastal" waters, with the result that there would be detrimental confusion, and it would create continued controversy, with the resultant annoyance to the department officials and all other interested parties.
As a case in point, the harbour of Vancouver, for some unknown reason, was illegally declared a minor inland water about twenty years ago, with the result that this automatically entitled men, whose experience on board a vessel might have been confined almost exclusively to collecting fares, to obtain minor water certificates and to take charge of passenger vessels carrying sometimes as many as five hundred passengers per trip, plying across waters where there is continually a heavy traffic of all kinds of craft, including many ocean liners and fast coastal vessels, under which conditions we consider the highest qualifications and experience is essential.
We do not think it is necessary to elaborate on the seriousness of such a situation in the event of an emergency, such as a collision, and the importance of proper training and experience where the lives of passengers are at stake.
Another view we take is that as long as a person or company complies with the letter of the law, they could successfully contest any action taken to prevent them from so operating.	*
We strongly urge that paragraph one of Bill 53 be withdrawn, as we consider it dangerous, for the reason that it could be construed to permit men without the necessary experience in these coastal waters to operate large passenger vessels almost anywhere on this coast.
It appears to us that the reason for the proposal to have "sheltered arms of the sea" classed as "minor" waters is to overcome the difficulty of providing for certificates for small

vessels carrying passengers and mail in some of our inlets. It seems to us that this has been, or could be, taken care of through the fact that it is proposed to create a new class of certificate for "steamship licensed as a ferry." Subsection P, paragraph 3, Bill 53.
These small boats could be classed as ferries and the rules could provide for certificates valid for ferries of over fifteen gross tons and for ferries under fifteen gross tons, respectively.
They go on to say:
We are firmly of the opinion that only responsible and experienced persons should be allowed to be in charge of a vessel carrying passengers for hire or gain, no matter how small the vessel may be, as it is. known that a number of these boats measured to register 4-90 to 4-99 gross tons frequently have as many as forty, or even more, passengers on board, crossing dangerous waters, in charge of only one youth employed by the owners of these vessels to act in the dual capacity of master and engineer. These youths apparently do not understand the risks they are taking, and it is safe to say, seldom have even a rudimentary knowledge of the rules of the road, nor could they be expected to handle an emergent condition such as a collision, or sinking as a result of overloading or stress of weather. Under the present laws such a person has nothing to lose and is not responsible to any marine authority.
We think that our suggestion that a certificate be provided for vessels of fifteen or twenty ross tons and under is the solution to this eretofore difficult matter, and should not work a hardship on anyone, while at the same time it would provide reasonable protection for the men, women and scores of children who often use this class of craft for transportation, sometimes over a distance of twenty miles, or more, across treacherous waters, they apparently having little or no understanding of the danger.
I submit that evidence coming from this source should be given great weight. I know the members of the guild have given this legislation and their brief their very earnest consideration, and are anxious to serve only the public interest and the public safety in this matter. I should add, in conclusion, that there is no longer any difficulty in securing certificated masters of the required standard and qualifications for work of this kind. Plenty of them are available for employment. I see no reason why this classification should apply in such a way as to lower the qualifications of masters or mates in charge of passenger carrying vessels.

I had not intended again to take part in this debate, but I really cannot allow some of the statements that have been made to go on the record without protest. We all know of the guild referred to by the hon. members and it would seem that either they do not understand the situation or else they are making a very ex parte statement. The association to which the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) referred
Canada Shipping Act

is an association of masters and mates. The members of this guild are quite naturally and properly looking after their own interests. Their interests are to see that a master and a mate are on every boat that goes out of a harbour on any occasion, but I do not know that we all look at this matter from their point of view. This will not mean that there will be more of them employed; it means that there will be fewer of them employed. That seems a broad statement to make, but it will work out like this: The law is and always has been that any vessel up to five tons does not require any certificated officer; anyone can take it out. Several of these small boats serve points where a man or a woman going to market wants to cross with three dozen eggs or something like that. Such a traffic will not stand a certificated master and mate. What would happen? They will get a boat of 4-9 tons and jam it full with all the people they can get on. The new provisions in the bill are intended to help to preserve the safety of life because men will be encouraged to use larger boats. I have heard men say that if it were possible to get a temporary certificate for a boat larger than five tons, they would build a bigger and safer boat with more powerful engines. Men will be encouraged to go after these temporary certificates and then they will be able to run larger and safer boats.
The hon. member has referred to a boy who usually takes up tickets being placed in charge of a boat carrying 500 passengers. Section 123 of the act describes who shall get temporary certificates, and it states that they shall be limited to people in charge of a boat carrying twelve passengers or under. That is what the section says, but 500 passengers has a much more pathetic sound. It is also limited to boats of twenty tons, not 8,000 tons. As the minister says, these boats are not going to be entrusted to someone who knows nothing but the taking up of tickets. The regulations call for an eye test, a hearing test, a colour blindness test, a knowledge of the rules of the road and some knowledge of signals.
Much has been said about the necessity of having a navigator to handle a boat in fogs, that there should be a man in charge capable of taking the boat anywhere in this hemisphere. During the war a lot of men from the Pacific coast served on the merchant ships taking troops to the old country. It was remarked by British seamen, than whom there are no finer or more expert in the world, how these men from the Pacific coast were able to find their way in total darkness. This was done by what is known as catching the echo. They would blow their whistle and then they

could tell from how long it took the echo to come back just where they were. Apparently this method is not studied on the other side and it was considered to be a very remarkable thing.
During the last campaign I had occasion to travel some fifteen miles at night in a fog so dense that I would have preferred to stay where I was. However I was very anxious to get away and the fog was so thick that when we had got ten yards from a wharf where there was a steamer of perhaps 9,000 tons, very brightly lighted, we could not see it. The man in charge of the boat upon which I was travelling probably did not have a master's ticket, but he knew every yard, so to speak, of those waters. He carried us along in good time without slackening speed except when there was danger of running into fishing nets. In a fog as bad as anything I have ever seen on the coast he landed us at the exact place we wanted to land. He was able to do this because he was familiar with this echo system. He could catch the echo and he knew when he had reached a certain place. He could make a turn when he should make a turn. That sort of local knowledge is worth far more than the ability to shoot the sun. When you are crossing a bay five miles in width you do not need to be able to shoot the sun.
The minister has told us that this practice has been in use for twenty-seven years and that at the present time there are not more than five temporary certificates on the Pacific coast. Apparently this practice has been going on illegally under a misapprehension, and it is now proposed to make the thing legal. I do not think there is any real danger such as has been suggested. The same men who have prescribed these regulations for inland or safe waters during all these years will presumably continue along the same lines. If we are going to be so fussy about these things, let us devote ourselves to something more practicable. Under section 133 of the act, a pleasure yacht does not need any master or mate. Any millionaire can put on a white cap with gold braid on it and call himself a captain. He very soon promotes himself to commodore. He can take his friends aboard and can sink the whole lot of them without any restriction whatever. He can ram a fishing boat or any other boat, but because his boat is a pleasure yacht he does not need to be a qualified captain. It does not matter whether his boat is five tons or 500 tons, he is free to go where he likes and do anything he likes. He does not need to have even

Canada Shipping Act
a boatswain on board. We might better deal with these questions instead of these other petty matters.
I can assure hon. members that instead of having certificated masters and mates on these boats making these short trips, they will not use boats of any size at all. They will be forced to use boats of 4-9 tons, and I know from personal experience that that size of boat is very uncomfortable when the water is a little rough. I give full credence to the good intentions of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). I have the greatest regard for this particular guild and I have fought their battles in this house when I thought they were right. However, they are looking at things very much from their own point of view and I am sure they will not be deprived of any means of livelihood by this amendment. It will only give the travelling public a safer means of travel.

Is it the intention of the
minister to use temporary certificates, or will he make the men who operate these boats in minor waters get proper certificates under the act? Apparently there is quite a difference in the test which they have to pass. If they will all be working under temporary certificates, that would not seem to be a very sound practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) was arguing on the principle that they had to get ordinary certificates. As I say, only five temporary certificates have been granted on the Pacific coast.
It is not the minister's intention to grant a lot of temporary certificates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

What qualifications will

Does the minister not think that the government is going rather far in this? Let it be remembered that this is a standard act. Perhaps I might recite briefly the history of the act. The general form of it was settled by the preceding administration. We employed counsel and drafted a bill which I toiok to England. not a ticket of competency; it is a temporary certificate known as a certificate of service. That depends upon his having served a period of time during a preceding number of years in a capacity for which he now seeks to obtain a certificate, but he has to undergo an examination.

speechtext: May I interrupt my right hon. friend for a moment; I think he is on the wrong section.

speechtext: But we have the old section 116 in there as well.

Certainly; I have section 116 before me, providing for the rights of holders of certificates. There are the four certificates, foreign-going, home trade, inland water and minor waters certificates. I was out of the chamber for a moment, but when we were dealing with the preceding section I was going to point out to the minister that there is nothing with reference to the physical ability of the man, his ability to see and to observe colours and signals. Surely that is of first consideration, but I notice that it is not in the bill. This is not a reflection upon the minister, of course-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is in the regulations.

That is the point exactly; it is in the regulations, but the other factors that are in the statute cannot be modified by ministerial regulations. Doubtful cases of this sort sometimes warrant the old maxim that bad cases make bad law, and cases of hardship sometimes make very bad administration, especially in a democracy. The point I am making at the moment in this connection, however, is that we should not go too far in our endeavour to meet cases that come to our attention. You cannot generalize in order to meet particular cases. I know that two years ago, when we passed this statute, cases were urged upon us, and we felt that when we provided for a man having satisfactory service for a period of one year during the ten years prior to 1931, we were going as far as we could within reason. I notice that in the new section the date has been made January 1, 1936.
In other words, if at any time since January 1, 1926, the man is able to prove that he has been a year in any of the several classes of service mentioned; if he has certificates,- issued under the regulations but not under the statute,-as to sobriety when he has been on board, as to satisfactory vision and ability to discern and read signals, and if he passes the prescribed examination he may get a certificate of service, which is not one of competency. It does not permit him, fortunately, under some of the sections, to be in charge of vessels that have to do with passengers, except in a very limited sense. Without following the matter up at any greater length for the time being, I suggest that we are going rather a long distance by placing in the hands of the minister a discretion which I think he himself would be the first to wish he did not possess. This is a new provision, as my hon. friend beside me notes, as far as the discretion is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I might say that there is always a little hardship in changing regulations. It has been represented to us that there are not more than about five boats that make occasional trips to the West Indies which would be concerned.
What class of boats?

speechtext:
Sailing boats, or boats
carrying sails and auxiliary powers. It is a temporary situation, and in order to avoid hardship in those few instances we felt that for the time being they should not be cut off overnight.
