Mr. Chairman, to me,
as to all hon. members of the committee, this is the most important of the three bills which deal with the problems of the returned men. This problem forms a very large part of the entire problem of unemployment; if we can solve one I believe we can solve the other, although I am not suggesting for a moment that the problem can be solved in its entirety. As we all know, many returned men would never seek pensions, never seek hospitalization, never seek assistance of any sort if it were not for the fact that the cards of life have been stacked against them. They played the game to the best of their ability, but through the peculiar trend of economic conditions are now the losers, and find themselves to a certain extent on the economic scrap heap. I have known of men who left Canada to fight for England in the Boer war; to-day they are nearing the end of life's trail, but

because they lived a few years too soon they were ineligible to take part in the war of 1914-18 and to-day are faced with poverty and starvation; yet they do not come under this act. It is, of course, very true that Canada has no responsibility towards these men. But they are good Canadians nevertheless, and I hope the Minister of Pensions will intercede very strongly on their behalf with the British Minister of Pensions when a favourable opportunity presents itself.
Then, again, there are men who served during the war of 1914-18 who were discharged as medically unfit; they went on farms; they have fought weeds, grasshoppers, drought, hail, and low prices, and to-day they are broken in health. They are a splendid class of citizens, and I think their problem should have the careful consideration of this commission.
One thing I find it difficult to understand is the reason for so many commissions being appointed by the present government. Ottawa has always been known as Ottawa the beautiful, but I think it will soon be known as the city of commissions. Really I think we are drifting into government by commission rather than government by executive council. In 1932 the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking to a resolution regarding the Salary Deduction Act, said:
I think we might well forego immediately the carrying out of some of the investigations that are being held at public expense.
I am wondering if he referred to commissions. However, we of this party are not offering any serious objection to this commission. We feel that this commission will be beneficial to the returned men. We feel that it differs from the regular type of commission, in that it has been given a definite mandate. It has been given a definite sum of money, approximately half a million dollars, and it is hoped that it will try out some project or projects, on a small scale perhaps, and at the end of twelve months show us a small working model of one of these plans. The members of this commission, by the nature of their appointment, can be very practical, while the other commission, the national employment commission, will have to be more or less theoretical. We hope that this half million dollars will not be squandered upon some silly experiment, but will be utilized on projects which will be really beneficial.
Finally I would urge upon the chairman of the commission that when he feels like making a peroration in public he refrain from copying the chairman of the national employ-

Veterans' Assistance Commission
ment commission. This gentleman in his first public utterance said:
Our government believes, and the national employment commission believes, that Canadians are ready to move out of this atmosphere of doubt and criticism. More, that they are prepared to take their part in a nationwide cooperative effort to face squarely the problems before us, and to make such sacrifices as will bring about their solution.
I want to stress that word "sacrifice." When I read that I thought there are very few sacrifices that the people of western Canada can make to-day. I felt like saying to the chairman of that commission, who is reputed to be a very rich man: "Go thou and do likewise."
For the next twelve months we shall watch with interest the work of the commission. We shall endeavour to refrain from criticizing, for we know they have a most difficult task and one that will tax their ingenuity and ability to the utmost.

I am afraid not.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: For the purpose of cleaning up as expeditiously as possible the many claims which are now pending it was thought advisable to ask the authority of parliament to name five additional ad hoc commissioners who would hold office for a year or less.

Veterans' Assistance Commission
chairman may from time to time direct. It is proposed that the commissioners shall be divided among different districts. On section 5-Jurisdiction of commission.

I do not know whether my observations should be made at this point, but I wish to say one or two things about an instance which came to my attention, and I am suggesting that some provision should be made against such contingencies. The soldier I have in mind went overseas and performed the duties of a soldier in France. After being gassed or wounded he came back and was not in receipt of a pension. In order to seek a livelihood he went to the United States, in which country he died not long ago. In order to prevent his being buried in a pauper's grave certain friends of his in my constituency borrowed the money to defray expenses of his burial. I have written the minister stating these facts and he replies that there is no provision whereby the friends of a soldier, once he has been buried, may obtain any money from the last post fund. In this instance a friend borrowed the money -and I know this, because I endorsed the note-in order to prevent the soldier's burial in a pauper's grave. Now the minister says, *"Oh, he is buried; we cannot touch it." I am asking the minister if he could reimburse the friend who had no legal obligation to bury the soldier. I am just wondering why a person who spends money in this way should not be reimbursed, and if he is not I wonder why the last post fund was created. It will not do for the minister to say that there may be abuses. In the particular instance I have cited I really do not see why some provision could not be made. I am fully aware of the overreaching of certain people because they were soldiers overseas, but I think the particular instance I have mentioned should not be barred.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I regret, Mr. Chairman, that the instance mentioned by my hon. friend from Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLennam) would not in any event come up under this legislation. As he is well aware, the last post fund is a fund which is not directly under the control of the government. A large num-

ber of very generous citizens have devoted their time and have raised large sums of money for the purpose of seeing to it that no ex-member of the forces is unable to find proper burial. This fund is operated under certain regulations, and I am glad to say that we have been able to make arrangements for the burial of our soldiers in the United States, which hitherto has not been possible. I had an instance some years ago similar to that mentioned by my hon. friend, and I was unable to obtain repayment of the amount whidh had been expended on the burial of that soldier. Perhaps, if that matter could be looked into and pressure brought to bear on -the last post fund, something might possibly be done, but I hardly think we could do it under the Pension Act.

I wanted to bring the instance before the minister to see if something could not be done, for I am sure if he were seized of the facte he would be sympathetic because in this instance they really couldi not afford to borrow the money to bury this soldier. Possibly some rule prevents anything being done in this instance, but sometimes rules are very illogical, and on this occasion the rule was not very logical. If this man were above ground he would be buried by the last post fund, but the moment he goes underneath the ground he does not come under the fund.

Subsection 2 of section 5 provides that if a pension has been improperly given, but not as a result of fraud or misrepresentation, and if a veteran has been -receiving the pension for not less than five years, it will not be cancelled if the commission considers that cancellation would result in hardship. What is the reason for this new provision? Of course, cancellation of a pension would always result in hardship after a man has -been receiving it, and it seems to me extraordinary that simply because a man has been receiving a pension improperly for any -reason at all, he should continue to receive it when it is found out that he ought never to have had it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In the early days of the work of the pension commission the number of claims that came in was, as one can readily understand, very great. T-hey were dealing with hundreds of claims, in fact, a hundred applications a day, away back in 1919 and 1920, and it can be readily understood that in some instances it was impossible to give them proper consideration.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Persons have been in receipt of a pension possibly ever since that time, and then owing to some accident or perhaps some review it was found that the pension was awarded and paid in error. Some instances which would have involved very considerable hardship were brought to the attention of the committee by the chairman of the commission himself. He felt that in some instances he could not cancel awards which had been made through error, and in order to make it quite clear that where undue hardship might ensue from cancellations, the commission would have discretion to continue the payment, and also to legalize the action of the chairman, the committee thought it was the proper thing to do to insert this amendment in the act. It is a departure, I quite admit, from ordinary legislation, but it must be remembered that this is remedial and beneficial legislation passed with the intent of bringing the greatest possible measure of justice to the ex-soldders and their dependents, and it was thought that a provision such as this should be recommended to parliament.

Have there not been instances where a veteran has been found to be receiving a pension larger than he was entitled to, receiving perhaps forty dollars a month when he should have received only twenty, and when the facts were ascertained has, not a certain amount been deducted from his pension each month until the overpayment had been returned to the government? Have there not been such instances?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think it is well known to hon. members that within the last two or three years there has been a large number of reviews of pensions and pension assessments, and a number of pensions have been decreased, but in no case of that kind was reimbursement required from the applicant. There have been claims, and quite a large number, for reimbursement when the payment had been received through fraud, but not when it was due to an error or when there had been an overassessment.
In the first line of page 4 of the reprinted bill has the word "five" been substituted for "ten"?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; in the reprinted bill it is five years.

I am not rising to raise any objection to this clause, but I would like .to say something about instances of real 'hardship that have come under my own observation quite frequently *of men who had undoubtedly served overseas and quite evidently sustained disabili-
12, 1936
Veterans' Assistance Commission
ties, but who through some error on the part of the soldier or some officer would be found disentitled to pension. Where there was some error or mistake on the part of the soldier or some officer, the soldier would be found to be disentitled to any pension. The rules have been carried out very strictly against a number of men known to me personally. If those who are entitled to pension but who do not come within the provisions of the law were treated with the same leniency as is contemplated by this section to be shown to men who are paid too much, I think this would remove a great deal of the dissatisfaction among soldiers. Within the week I had a letter from a man who served through the war. He was in the big drive of 1918 and came home badly wounded and suffered considerable hardship in the hospital in Halifax. I know he is not exaggerating his condition, but he is getting only a miserably small pension because of what I believe was a faulty examination in the early history of his application. To my mind that is a clear case of underpayment, but I cannot find any such lenient treatment as seems to be exhibited to those who are paid too much.

As a result of the
revision to which the minister has just referred, was there not a considerable number of instances where the pensions were stopped, not where pensions had been fraudulently granted but where they had been granted by mistake?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; there was a considerable number.
This revision having taken place in 1934, those pensioners have not received their pensions, but where the discovery is made in 1936 and subsequent years, they will continue to get their pensions.

I know of a large number of instances in which pension was discontinued because of error in the application and I .think there were instances in which the money was returned. I only want to ask the minister if it is dear that in no case where a pension was awarded by error had there been any return of money to the department. If that is so, then that difficulty is cleared up. I cannot help but refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). I am sure that the result will be that applications will be made to continue these men on the pension list. That will be the inevitable result of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I do not think they could
come under this legislation, but I recognize that there is a possibility of such claims being made. Those instances were not brought to the attention of the committee. We did not deal with them, but perhaps that is no excuse for not taking them up at .this time. Had the members of the committee been aware that there was any considerable number of claims, such as .those mentioned by the bon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), perhaps provision would have been made for them.

Does the minister say that
he is advised that in no instance has there been a claim made for the repayment of pension?

There have been claims
made for repayment?

speechtext:
Not in instances of error;
there have been claims made in instances of fraudulent misrepresentation.
But where it was done innocently?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am informed, no.

That is different from my information. There are quite a few instances within my knowledge, many of which arose in connection with the claim of a wife who could not produce the death certificate of her husband.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We are now entering into another subject altogether, the so-called disputed marriage cases. In a large number of these, where the wives were asked for marriage certificates, it was found that there had been no marriage. Payment should never have been made, but that was not an error of judgment on the part of the commission that awarded the pension; it was just a matter of misrepresentation, although perhaps in good faith. In certain instances good faith was shown, such as a remarriage in the anticipation of a divorce which had not yet taken place. In nearly all such instances the commission awarded pension, and in others repayment of moneys overpaid was not asked. I think there are some sixty odd cases remaining for disposal out of a total of 800. Most of them have been definitely settled.

Section agreed to.

On section 7-Four members.
Will the minister explain the reason for adding another member to the appeal court?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Representations were made by certain ex-soldier organizations that the appeal court was giving a too strict and too narrow interpretation to the law. As my right hon. friend knows, this court is composed of two lawyers and a former judge of the supreme court. It was thought that the presence on the board of a man familiar with medical questions might be of some assistance to the board and might serve to mitigate what was considered to be undue severity on the part of the board. Perhaps this does not refer to this particular section, but I should like to say a word or two about this appeal court. This court has had a very difficult task to perform. When cases reach them they have been before the pension commission. Sometimes a case may have been considered time and time again by the commission before being sent to the court. In most instances when a case does reach the appeal court it is very difficult of decision in favour of the applicant. As is well known, there has been throughout the country considerable criticism of the appeal court, and it was felt that if a member of the medical profession were placed on the court he might be in a position to understand better the medical questions which are very often the principal factors in arriving at a decision.
Is it permissible to ask who the minister proposes to appoint to the court?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have been too busy trying to get this legislation through and discussing matters with members of the committee to consider the appointment which will follow the passing of this bill.
What will happen in a court of four when they are divided?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Only three can serve at
one time. There will be a spare member of the court. Section 67, subsection 1 reads:
Any two members of the court shall constitute a quorum and may lawfully hear and dispose of any appeal brought before the court.

It will be remembered that in England-I heard the Minister of Pensions himself say so-they attributed the success of their operations entirely to the fact that having arrived at a period they stuck to it,
With certain exceptions.
We have changed it in every parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I believe that from 1919 the date has been changed at least five times, and in 1930 the time limits were removed altogether, so that every man who had had a claim, whether it had been passed upon or not, whether he had been debarred or not, was allowed to make a new application and put in a new claim. They have had six years in which to put these claims before the commission.
That is what made the duty of the appeal court so difficult.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Exactly.
It must be remembered that in Britain while they had a fixed date, they were always ready to consider any applications-
It was left to the discretion of the minister.
Which he seldom exercised.

Paragraph (b) has a proviso:
Provided always that the appeal division may, in its discretion, with respect to this class, grant leave to have the application entertained after the first day of January, 1938.
It is now 1940. What is the significance of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The commission has the discretion to grant leave. Unless a dead line were put in, every claim would be entertained. Now, a claim can be entertained only after leave is obtained from the commission.

This is the only clause that relates to section 22 of the bill. Some time ago I called the attention of the minister to the fact that there were a few instances of returned soldiers having no children of their own, who had adopted foster children. There is no clarification by the amendment, but I am again urging that subsection 4, which gives the commission discretionary power in the awarding of pensions in respect of any children entitled, in the opinion of the commission, to be maintained by a member of the forces in respect of whom pension is claimed, shall be liberally interpreted to include such instances, and particularly in regard to education. I know of several men who, having no children of their own, adopted foster children and the foster children have been debarred from the grant to aid them in obtaining education.
